title: The Stoned Age
onscreen: Altered states, curiosity, and the long history of making meaning.
notes: Open with “Please turn to page 666.” Pause. Explain that the title is an invitation to investigate, not a claim that drugs explain everything. Introduce Root Sequence as coordinator and this as an AI-assisted draft.

title: Four questions, not one
onscreen: What happened? What does it mean? What supports it? Who gets authority?
notes: Use the fictional dream example. Ask the audience to notice how quickly “it felt true” becomes “it is true.” Do not ask people to disclose drug use or intimate experiences.

title: Archaeology cannot interview the smoke
onscreen: Material traces give us local evidence.
notes: Briefly contrast Arad and the Pamirs. Emphasize residues and context; neither supplies the origin of religion. Show conceptual windows, not fabricated excavation imagery.

title: An object is not a recipe
onscreen: A bundle and a hair sample answer different questions.
notes: Contrast the South American bundle with Menorca hair. Keep exposure, preparation and interpretation distinct. Refer detailed analytical claims to the paper.

title: The ape needs more evidence
notes: Explain the missing causal chain in the strongest stoned-ape claim. Distinguish temporary cognitive change from biological evolution. Present the published hypothesis as a hypothesis.

title: The idea feels brilliant
onscreen: Generation and evaluation need separate measures.
notes: Distinguish acute subjective insight from lower task performance. At seven days, self-rated novelty increased while convergent thinking remained lower than placebo. New to the participant does not mean independently verified originality. Avoid general cognitive-upgrade claims.

title: Meaning is already something
onscreen: Personal significance is not a cosmic certificate.
notes: Keep reports of meaning distinct from metaphysical verification. Explain that a physiological account need not dismiss personal importance. Do not describe the research as proving religion either true or false. Note the small screened sample, supported setting and acute fear alongside significance.

title: Nobody makes meaning alone
onscreen: Stories have audiences, teachers and critics.
notes: Introduce the editorial experience-to-revision map. Context matters; it is not a universal sequence. Ask who is allowed to correct a shared account.

title: Who owns the explanation?
notes: Discuss the difference between acknowledging testimony and authorizing decisions over others. Introduce IPCI as one organization with a situated position, not a representative of all Indigenous peoples.

title: The oracle has autocomplete
notes: Define the AI analogy narrowly as evaluation of compelling interpretations. Cite sycophancy research as bounded evidence. Do not equate AI outputs with human consciousness or psychedelic states. The cited evaluation is the 2023 version and does not describe every current model.

title: What would change our minds?
onscreen: Better sources. Better contrasts. Serious objections.
notes: Name the next research steps: full archaeological extraction, study appraisal, cultural scholarship and a bounded AI question. Explain that no human experiment has been run.

title: Keep the question open
onscreen: The universe has not supplied a foreword.
notes: Close with the project invitation. Use the final four minutes for discussion: what separates meaningful experience from shared knowledge? What would a respectful correction look like? Offer paper and source links.
